IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF EL PASO ELECTRIC                       )
COMPANY FOR                                                                )

STEPHEN FISCHMANN’S MOTION TO COMPEL

EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY’S

RESPONSES TO FISCHMANN DISCOVERY REQUESTS 1-1 AND 1-2

AND BRIEF IN SUPPORT



Intervenor Stephen Fischmann (“Fischmann”), appearing pro se, pursuant to 1.2.2.12 and

1.2.2.25(J) NMAC and Rules 1-026, 1-033, 1-034, and 1-037 NMRA, moves the Hearing

Examiners for an order compelling El Paso Electric Company (“EPE”) to provide complete

responses and responsive materials to Fischmann Discovery Requests 1-1 and 1-2. The

requests seek EPE-specific valuation information concerning the investment in EPE held

through Infrastructure Investments Fund (“IIF”) and its holding-company structure. That

information bears directly on the central cost-of-equity issue EPE itself has placed before the

Commission.


EPE’s amended cost-of-capital testimony states that the terms “ROE” and “cost of equity” are

used interchangeably, that a 10.00% to 11.40% range reflects “investors’ required return for an

equity investment in EPE,” and that 10.70% is a just and reasonable estimate of EPE’s cost of

equity. Amended Filing Direct Testimony of Jennifer E. Nelson (“Nelson Amended Direct”) at 3-

4, 9. Discovery Request 1-1 seeks, for valuations of the EPE investment, the discount rate and

valuation conclusion and the component inputs used to determine that rate, including capital
 structure, cost of debt, risk-free rate, beta, equity risk premium, and cost of equity. Request 1-2

seeks the corresponding audited-financial-statement disclosures of significant unobservable

inputs used to measure the EPE investment at fair value. This discovery is relevant to investor

return and risk inputs on which EPE’s ROE case rests. This discovery would consist of

contemporaneous valuations of the same EPE equity investment, and the assumptions used in

those valuations, can test, corroborate, distinguish, or impeach EPE’s assertions concerning

the return investors require for an equity investment in EPE.


MOTION


1.     On July 13, 2026, Fischmann served his First Set of Discovery Requests on EPE

pursuant to 1.2.2.25 NMAC. A complete copy of the requests and EPE’s objections are

attached as Exhibit A, as required by 1.2.2.25(J)(2) NMAC.


2.     Discovery Request 1-1 asks, for each valuation of the EPE investment performed by or

for IIF since the July 29, 2020 closing, for the discount rate(s), resulting valuation conclusion,

workpapers/models/calculation files, and specified inputs and methodologies, including capital-

structure weights, cost of debt, risk-free rate, beta, equity risk premium, and cost of equity.

Request 1-2 asks for the note to the audited financial statements of IIF (or the master

partnership holding the EPE investment) for each fiscal year since closing that discloses

significant unobservable inputs used to measure the EPE investment at fair value and the

basis of measurement and reporting. Ex. A.


3.     EPE did not provide substantive answers. It objected that the requests are overly broad,

burdensome, irrelevant, seek information from entities not parties to this proceeding, and in the

case of Request 1-1 are a “compound interrogatory.” EPE also invoked general objections

concerning privilege, confidentiality, voluminous information, and possession, custody, or

control. See Exhibit A.
 4. On August 5, 2026, Fischmann requested a conference concerning the objections and

identified the issues he believed required resolution, including relevance to EPE’s requested

ROE, EPE’s ability to obtain IIF-related records, burden, the number and location of responsive

valuations, the “compound interrogatory” objection, and confidentiality. The parties thereafter

scheduled and held a Zoom conference on August 21, 2026. The email chain is attached as

Exhibit B.


5. Fischmann’s September 2, 2026 email memorializing the August 21 conference states that

EPE’s counsel indicated that some 2025 investor rate-of-return reporting was available to EPE

and could be produced, but that EPE did not believe it was required to obtain affiliate records

concerning cost of capital and investment returns. Ex. B. Fischmann supports his recollection

of the conference by the Affidavit attached as Exhibit C. Ex. C ¶ 5. As of the date of this

motion, EPE has not produced that 2025 material. Ex. C ¶ 7.


6. The Commission's July 16, 2026 Sua Sponte Order required EPE to “contemporaneously

supplement all discovery responses that are affected by the Amended Application.” July 16,

2026 Sua Sponte Order ¶ E(8). The same Order preserved discovery already served and

provided that the stay did not relieve EPE of its continuing obligation to respond completely

and accurately to outstanding discovery or to supplement prior responses as required by

Commission rules. The August 27, 2026 Order Establishing Revised Procedural Schedule

likewise provides that “[a]ll parties have an ongoing obligation to respond to discovery as

required by Commission rules.” Aug. 27, 2026 Order ¶ D. Staff and intervenor direct testimony

is due October 23, 2026. ¶ I. Prompt resolution is therefore necessary so that responsive

information can be evaluated before testimony is filed.


7. The participants made a good-faith effort to resolve the dispute, including written exchanges

and the August 21 conference, and were unable to do so. See 1.2.2.25(J)(3) NMAC.
 8. Before filing, positions on this Motion were requested from other parties and staff. The city

of Las Cruces, Dona Ana County, CCAE, Phillip Simpson, and Dwight Eggers state they

support the motion. DOD/FEA, Walmart, DOJ, and PRC Staff state they take no position. No

other responses have been received.


RELIEF REQUESTED


Fischmann respectfully requests an order:


A. compelling EPE, within five business days after entry of the order, to provide complete,

request-by-request answers to Discovery Requests 1-1 and 1-2 and to produce all

nonprivileged responsive materials within EPE’s possession, custody, or control;


B. specifically requiring production of any 2025 or other investor-return, valuation, fair-value, or

related reporting concerning the EPE investment that EPE has received or can obtain and that

is responsive to Requests 1-1 or 1-2;


C. requiring EPE, for responsive EPE-investment materials held by IIF US 2, Sun Jupiter, IIF,

JPMIM, or another entity, to make a reasonable inquiry into EPE’s practical ability to obtain the

materials and, if EPE continues to assert lack of control, to identify the inquiry made, the entity

or custodian asked, the categories of materials sought, and the factual basis for EPE’s

assertion that it cannot procure them;


D. requiring EPE to comply with Rule 1-034(B) NMRA by stating whether each response

includes all responsive materials and, for any materials withheld based on an objection,

describing with reasonable particularity what is being withheld for each objection;


E. granting such other relief as is just and necessary to permit Fischmann to prepare testimony

by the October 23, 2026 deadline.


BRIEF IN SUPPORT
        Intervenor Stephen Fischmann (“Fischmann”), appearing pro se, submits this Brief in

Support of his Motion to Compel Discovery from EPE.


I. Governing Discovery Standard


Commission policy “favors prompt and complete disclosure and exchange of information” and

encourages timely discovery so parties can make effective hearing presentations rather than

use cross-examination as a discovery device. 1.2.2.25(A) Rule 1-026(B)(1) NMRA permits

discovery of nonprivileged information relevant to the subject matter of the action; the

information need not itself be admissible if it appears reasonably calculated to lead to

admissible evidence. The responding party must provide all nonprivileged responsive

information then known to it, subject to the rule’s limitations. Rule 1-026(B)(2).


New Mexico construes discovery broadly. United Nuclear Corp. v. General Atomic Co., 1980-

NMSC-094, 96 N.M. 155, 629 P.2d 231. In construing Rules 1-033 and 1-034, the Supreme

Court rejected formalistic limits that disregard “the policy of liberal discovery and the practical

realities of the particular situation.” Id. ¶¶ 54-58. That same practical approach governs EPE’s

contention that responsive EPE-investment records may reside with entities elsewhere in its

ownership structure.


II. The Requested EPE-Investment Valuation Information Is Relevant to EPE’s Requested

ROE


The relevance issue can be resolved from EPE’s own affirmative case. Nelson states that her

purpose is to recommend EPE’s ROE and assess EPE’s requested capital structure. Nelson

Amended Direct at 3. She expressly states that “ROE” and “cost of equity” are used

interchangeably in her testimony, and that a range of 10.00% to 11.40% reflects “investors’

required return for an equity investment in EPE.” Id. at 3-4. She recommends 10.70% as EPE’s

cost of equity. Id. at 4, 9.
 EPE’s ROE analysis uses the DCF, CAPM/ECAPM, and risk-premium approaches. Id. at 9. Its

CAPM analysis uses a risk-free rate, beta coefficients, and a market risk premium. Id. at 64-66.

EPE also asks the Commission to approve a capital structure of 55.50% equity and 44.50%

debt. Id. at 4. Request 1-1 asks what discount rate and valuation result IIF actually used when

valuing the EPE investment and asks for the component assumptions used in those valuations,

including capital structure, cost of debt, risk-free rate, beta, equity risk premium, and cost of

equity. Exhibit A. The overlap is not incidental.


A private-fund valuation discount rate is not necessarily the same economic quantity as a

regulatory ROE. It may reflect acquisition premium, parent-level leverage, taxes, liquidity, or

other valuation conventions. That is why the underlying assumptions and methodology matter.

Discovery can show whether and why the contemporaneous valuation of the same EPE equity

investment uses materially different investor-return or risk assumptions from those EPE asks

the Commission to adopt for ratemaking. That information may corroborate EPE’s case,

support adjustment, or supply a basis for cross-examination and rebuttal. Each possibility

satisfies the discovery standard.


The adopted acquisition decision also confirms that IIF/Sun Jupiter investment returns and

EPE’s regulatory ROE are not categorically unrelated. In the Hearing Examiner’s Amended

Certification of Stipulation, subsequently adopted by the Commission’s Final Order Adopting

Amended Certification of Stipulation dated March 11, 2020, the Hearing Examiner explained

that, because IIF US 2 and Sun Jupiter could not recover the acquisition premium through

rates, “their actual return on the purchase price, including the premium, can be expected to be

lower than the targeted return on equity that the Commission establishes in an EPE base rate

case.” Amended Certification of Stipulation at 56, Case No. 19-00234-UT (Feb. 12, 2020),

adopted by Final Order Adopting Amended Certification of Stipulation (Mar. 11, 2020). The

adopted Amended Certification therefore expressly analyzes the relationship between the

owner’s return on the EPE investment and EPE’s authorized ROE.
 III. EPE’s Overbreadth and Burden Objections Do Not Justify Withholding All

Responsive Information


EPE relies on Archuleta v. Santa Fe Police Department ex rel. City of Santa Fe, 2005-NMSC-

006, 137 N.M. 161, 108 P.3d 1019. Archuleta does not support a categorical refusal here.

There the request sought every suspension, demotion, or termination of any police officer of

any rank for five years, and the request gave the hearing officer no guidance for determining

which cases were similar or more egregious. Id. ¶ 23. The Supreme Court held that the request

was overly broad, did not provide adequate guidance as to allow for a determination of what

was actually requested, and the requested material was only minimally relevant or irrelevant.

Id. ¶¶ 23-25. That does not describe the situation here.


Requests 1-1 and 1-2 identify one investment, the equity investment in EPE, and one recurring

event, the valuation of that investment, and a defined post-closing period. Request 1-1 further

identifies the precise valuation inputs sought. Request 1-2 seeks a specified financial-

statement disclosure for each fiscal year. Unlike Archuleta, the requests give both EPE and the

Hearing Examiners concrete guidance as to what documents and data are responsive and why

they matter.


EPE has failed to provide a factual record supporting the alleged burden of providing discovery.

Rule 1-034 requires a responding party to state “whether the response includes all responsive

materials. If the responding party withholds any responsive materials based on an objection,

the objection shall clearly describe with reasonable particularity what materials are being

withheld for each objection.” Rule 1-034(B) NMRA. The Committee Commentary to this Rule

explains,


The 2021 amendments to Rule 1-034(B) require the responding party “state whether the

response includes all responsive materials,” and, if it does not, the responding party “clearly

describe with reasonable particularity what materials are being withheld for each objection.”
 The purpose of this amendment is to disincentivize, if not eliminate, obfuscation of the

existence, volume, or nature of documents withheld from a production, or the basis for doing

so, through the interposition of objections. The default response to a request for production is

the production of responsive materials. While withholding documents pursuant to objections is

often legitimate, failure to divulge that material documents have been withheld, failure to

identify what materials have been disclosed, and failure to clearly state the reasons for

withholding materials is not.




EPE violates Rule 1-034(B) and in doing so demonstrates the very need for the Rule as

identified in the commentary. EPE’s go-to objection is to claim responding is burdensome

without ever complying with the rule’s requirement to actually demonstrate this

burdensomeness. The consequence of non-compliance and obfuscation should be to require

prompt production of improperly withheld materials. EPE’s objections are not supported with

concrete information concerning matters such as retention, locations searched, custodians,

search methodology, and the nature and volume of withheld material. EPE’s specific objections

provide no number of valuations, no estimate of responsive documents, no description of

custodians or locations, and no estimate of time or cost. Exhibit A. During the meet-and-confer

process, Fischmann was unable to determine who possessed the files, how many valuations

existed, how many documents were involved, and whether the files were scattered or

organized. EPE had not inquired with relevant affiliates, and did not respond to these

documented questions. Exhibt B.


IV. Corporate Separateness Does Not Resolve “Possession, Custody, or Control”; the

Governing Inquiry Is EPE’s Practical Ability to Obtain the EPE-Investment Materials
 EPE’s specific objection states that the requests seek information “from entities not a party to

this proceeding.” Exhibit A. This is not a valid objection. This rationale was rejected in United

Nuclear, where the Court stated,


{58} It is undisputed that neither United nor I&M was capable of procuring on its own the

information and documents sought from the partners. Thus, the critical inquiry concerns only

the first of the above mentioned principles—whether the party from whom the materials are

sought has the practical ability to obtain those materials. Because the inquiry is a pragmatic

one, the phrases “available” and “possession, custody or control” should not be subjected to

formalistic strictures which ignore the policy of liberal discovery and the practical realities of the

particular situation at issue. See Hart v. Wolff, supra, 489 P.2d at 117. Thus, it is immaterial

under Rules 33 and 34 that the party subject to the discovery orders does not own the

documents, or that it did not prepare or direct the production of the documents, or that it does

not have actual physical possession of them. It is also clear that the mere fact that the

documents are in the possession of an individual or entity which is different or separate from

that of the named party is not determinative of the question of availability or control. United

Nuclear, 1980-NMSC-094, ¶ 58.




The New Mexico Supreme Court held that the “critical inquiry” is whether the responding party

has the practical ability to obtain the materials. The Court explained that ownership,

preparation, actual physical possession, and the fact that documents are held by a different or

separate entity are not determinative. The inquiry is pragmatic and turns on the actual business

relationship and ability to procure the materials.


Under the United Nuclear holding, EPE must produce the requested discovery. First, the

information sought here concerns the valuation of EPE itself by the investment structure that

acquired and holds EPE. Second, the Hearing Examiner’s Amended Certification, adopted by
 the Commission’s March 11, 2020, Final Order, identifies IIF US 2 and Sun Jupiter as the

acquisition/holding-company entities and includes commitments specifically addressing access

to records. Among them, “IIF US 2 will provide the Commission access to its books and

records, as well as those of its applicable affiliates, as necessary to facilitate the Commission’s

audit or review of any affiliate transactions.” Amended Certification at 53-54, Case No. 19-

00234-UT. That commitment demonstrates that the materials sought concern EPE and entities

within EPE’s ownership structure and supports a factual inquiry into EPE’s practical ability to

obtain EPE-specific valuation materials. Third, Fischmann memorialized that during the August

21 conference EPE’s counsel stated some 2025 investor rate-of-return reporting was available

to EPE and could be produced. Exhibit B; Exhibit C ¶ 5. EPE has not produced that material.

Ex. C ¶ 7. At a minimum, any responsive material already available to EPE is not insulated

merely because it originated with an owner, holding company, fund, or investment manager.


V. The “Compound Interrogatory” Objection Does Not Excuse a Response


Rule 1-033(A) NMRA permits up to fifty written interrogatories “including all discrete subparts”

without leave. EPE does not state that Fischmann exceeded fifty interrogatories. Nor does it

identify a rule providing that an interrogatory becomes objectionable merely because related

subparts request the inputs and methodology necessary to understand one valuation subject.

Request 1-1 organizes related information under the single subject of each valuation of the

EPE investment. Even counting every listed subpart separately, EPE’s objection does not

demonstrate that the Rule 1-033 numerical limit has been exceeded.


VI. Cantrell Does Not Convert These Specific Existing Valuation Records into a “Fishing

Expedition”


EPE also cites Cantrell v. W & C Contracting Co., Inc., 1991-NMCA-091, 112 N.M. 609, 817

P.2d 1251, to characterize the requests as a fishing expedition. Fischmann’s requests are

material and relevant to the issues presented in this application, not random attempts to
 produce something useful. The requested discovery includes requests for valuations of the

EPE investment and audited-financial-statement notes disclosing the inputs used to measure

that investment at fair value. The relevance is clear and the discovery sought is targeted;

EPE’s own testimony asks the Commission to determine the investor-required return on an

equity investment in EPE. That is ordinary merits discovery.


VII. Confidentiality Is a Basis for Protection, Not for Categorical Nonproduction


EPE’s general objections invoke commercially sensitive, trade-secret, confidential, and

proprietary information. Exhibit A. Fischmann does not seek public disclosure of legitimately

protected material. Rule 1-026(C) NMRA and 1.2.2.25(K) NMAC authorize protective

conditions, and Section 62-6-17(C) establishes a procedure for Commission protection of

confidential or proprietary records. The Commission has, in fact entered a protective order

making EPE’s objections completely superfluous, and in bad faith.


VIII. EPE Must At Least Produce the Unobjectionable Portion and Identify What It Is

Withholding


Rule 1-034(B) requires a response to each item or category, specific reasons for objections,

specification of any part objected to, a statement whether the response includes all responsive

materials, and a reasonably particular description of materials withheld for each objection.

EPE’s objections do not disclose whether it searched for responsive EPE-investment materials,

what EPE already possesses, what it can obtain, how many valuations or financial-statement

notes exist, what categories are being withheld, or what portion could be produced without

burden. Exhibit A.


That deficiency is especially significant because Rule 1-026(B)(1) requires the responding

party to provide all nonprivileged responsive information then known to it, subject to applicable

limitations. Even if EPE maintains some objections, it should be compelled to produce the
 responsive portions not dependent on those objections and to explain with the specificity Rule

1-034 requires what remains withheld.


CONCLUSION


The motion should be granted and EPE ordered to produce the improperly withhold discovery.

EPE has placed the investor return on an equity investment in EPE at the center of this rate

case. Fischmann seeks contemporaneous EPE-specific valuation inputs and results that may

illuminate or test that issue. EPE’s objections do not justify withholding all responsive

information, and its corporate-separateness objection does not answer the governing practical

control inquiry. Fischmann therefore requests the Hearing Examiner grant his request, and

Order EPE to produce improperly withheld discovery responses promptly so as to allow their

use in formulating Direct Testimony.


Respectfully submitted,




/s/ Stephen Fischmann


Stephen Fischmann, Intervenor Pro Se

Mesilla Park, NM 88047


505-273-4956

Instructions and Definitions for Interrogatories, Requests for Production of Documents,
and Other Discovery

INTRODUCTION

Stephen Fischmann requests, pursuant to 1.2.2.25 NMAC, that you answer the
following Interrogatories and produce all documents which are responsive in any way to
the Interrogatories or in any way to the specific Requests for Production of Documents.
Your responses must be made in accordance with the following instructions and
definitions. If you have any questions about any of the Interrogatories or Requests for
Production, please contact the undersigned Staff Counsel.

Please serve responses by email to Stephen Fischmann and the official certificate of
service for this Case. Please also file the certificate of service for your responses (not
the discovery response itself) pursuant to the Commission's electronic filing policy, such
filing to be made with the Records Bureau of the New Mexico Public Regulation
Commission.

DEFINITIONS:

1. "The Company" and "EPE" refers to the Applicant, El Paso Electric Company, and
includes, but is not limited to, any and all of its attorneys, officers, consultants, agents,
employees, directors, representatives, officials, departments, divisions, subsidiaries,
predecessors, affiliates, or parent companies.
 "Staff' means the Staff of the Utility Division of the New Mexico Public Regulation
Commission, and "Commission" means the New Mexico Public Regulation

Commission.
2. The term "and/or" must be construed disjunctively or conjunctively as necessary so
that the scope of these interrogatories is as broad as possible to include any information
     that might be construed to be outside the scope of a singularly disjunctive or conjunctive
    request.

    3. "Agreement" means any contract, written or oral, or any non-contractual
    understanding.

    4. "Application" means El Paso Electric's: (1) Revision of its Retail Rates Under Advice
    Notice No. 317; and (2) Other Associated Relief, which is docketed by the Commission
    as Case No. 25-00082-UT.

    5. "Communication" is to be construed broadly and includes, but is not limited to,
    any oral or written statement, email, SMS message, dialogue, telephone
    conversation, discussion, or any conversation between or among persons by any
    means whatsoever.

    6. "Date" means the exact day, month, and year, if ascertainable, or if not, the best
    approximation of the day, month, and year available in relation to the events which are
    the subject of the Interrogatory or Request for Production.

    7. To "describe" means to relate as completely as possible each and every act,
    forbearance to act, omission, incident, event, condition, circumstance, or thing relating
    directly or indirectly to the subject of the description, including all pertinent dates.

    8. The term "document" is to be construed broadly and liberally to include
    "correspondence" and means every recording, including visual or auditory recordings,
    or electronic data recorded on a data server, of any information including, but not
    limited to, letters, handwritten messages, text messages, email communications,
    notices, memoranda, photographs, drawings, handwritten notes, books, periodicals,
    pamphlets, exhibits, pleadings, calendars, canceled checks, schedules, tax returns,
•   charts, maps, minutes, logs, graphs, financial statements, computer tapes,
    computer printouts, computer disks, USB drives, microfilm, and any other records of
    conversations, meetings, conferences, or seminars, and the like, as well as
    reproductions or copies of the documents, if the original is not available and only if the
    copy is an identical duplicate of the original document.
 1o. "Employee" includes your employees, consultants, or agents, including, but not
limited to, independent or consulting firms retained by you, beginning at the time this
case was docketed by the Commission.

11. "Explain" means to make known in detail, to make clear the cause or reason of, and
to account for each act, omission, incident, event, condition, circumstance, decision, or
thing relating directly or indirectly to, the subject of the explanation, including all
pertinent dates.

12. "Identification of a document" means to state, with respect to each document, as
appropriate: (a) the date of the document; (b) the title of the document; (c) the identity
of the person by whom or for whom the document was written or prepared; (d) the
identity of the person to whom the document was addressed or delivered; (e) the
general subject matter of the document; (f) the identity of the person having custody of
the original of the document, if a copy is provided; and (g) if any document was once in
your possession but is not now, the present location of the document, and the name
and address of the person who has possession of the original document.

13. "Identification of a person" means stating the person's full name, business address,
telephone number, email address, present position, and prior connection or association
with any party to the proceeding.

14. 11Person11means every natural person, corporation, partnership, association, joint
venture, cooperative, municipality, commission, governmental body, agency, or other
applicable business organization or entity.

15. "Records" includes the singular and the plural and means any regular, formal or
informal, official or unofficial, memorandum, document or written preservation of any
events, actions taken or rejected, decisions, and details relating to the subject matter of
the Interrogatory or Request for Production, and your response to those records. A
reproduction or copy of the original will suffice only if the original is not available and
only if the copy is an identical duplicate of the original. A statement of the substance of
the record will ouffioe only if a copy of the original is not availabl@. If you submit sither a
copy of the original or a statement of the substance of the record, please explain in
detail why the original or a copy, as may be applicable, is not available.

16. Whenever appropriate in order to bring within the scope of each Interrogatory or
Request for Production all responses which might otherwise be considered beyond the
scope of the Interrogatory or Request for Production: (a) the singular form of a word
should be interpreted as plural and the plural form of a word should be interpreted as
singular; (b) the use of the verb in any tense will be construed as the use of the verb in
any other appropriate tense; and (c) the masculine will be deemed to include the
 feminine, neuter, or other non-gender description, and the feminine, neuter, or other
non-gender description will be deemed to include the masculine.
INSTRUCTIONS:

This set of discovery may include Interrogatories, Requests for Production of
documents and things and entry upon land for inspection and other purposes,
Requests for Admissions, and other applicable discovery request mechanisms as
governed by the New Mexico Rules of Civil Procedure for the District Courts pertaining
to discovery, and as may be permitted by Commission Rule 1.2.2.25 NMAC.

1. Interrogatories must be answered with particularity and in detail.

2. Interrogatories must be answered separately and fully in writing, following
the identification form (i.e., numbering or lettering) elicited by the interrogatory
propounded.

3. Interrogatories must be answered under oath or affirmation, as may be authorized
under the law of the State of New Mexico and the Commission's Rules.

4. Interrogatories must be signed by hand and then scanned, or electronically, as may
be authorized under the law of the State of New Mexico and the Commission's Rules,
by the person or persons upon whose personal knowledge the responses are based, or
who participated in formulating the answer to the discovery.

5. You must provide the names of any other persons upon whose personal knowledge
answers or responses are based or who formulated the answer to the Interrogatories or
the response to a Request for Production or Request for Admission.

6. As part of your answers to this discovery, you must produce all relevant documents
and data by attachment, identifying with specificity which documents correspond to
which specific answers.

7. Answers to these Interrogatories are continuing in nature. In the event that any
information provided in an answer changes or is supplemented by future developments
or other factors, you must file appropriate supplemental answers as required by
Commission Rule 1.2.2.25(1) NMAC.

8. In answering Interrogatories and Requests for Production, you should furnish
all information which is in your possession, custody, or control including, but not limited
to, information from any files, records, or documents in the possession of your
attorneys, consultants, staff, accountants, experts, employees, former employees, and
other agents.
 9. This discovery should be answered based on your personal knowledge, the personal
knowledge of your attorneys, consultants, staff, accountants, experts, employees,
former employees, and any other agents, as appropriate or available, and with
reference to the sources described above.

1o. If the person providing the answer or response is not a witness who has filed written
direct testimony, please indicate which witnesses will be prepared to answer these
questions on the stand.

11. Please provide an electronic copy of your answers to this discovery request in
Microsoft Word. If any part of your answers were prepared using any spreadsheet
software, please provide an electronic copy of that part of your answer in Microsoft
Excel format.

12. If, after exercising due diligence, you are unable to answer any Interrogatory or to
